**Synthesist** (noun) is derived from combining the verb _synthesize_ with the suffix _-ist_. It traces back to the ancient Greek _σύνθεσις_ (a putting together or combining) and the classical Latin _synthesis_. The earliest recorded use of the word in English dates to the 1860s, notably appearing in the writings of botanist John G. Baker. [[1](https://www.oed.com/dictionary/synthesist_n), [2](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/synthesist), [3](https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2017/08/synthesizer.html), [4](https://www.facebook.com/GreekResidency/videos/greek-residency-synthesis/480223053769472/)]

The term has two distinct definitions and is generally found in specialized or niche literature rather than everyday speech: [[1](https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/synthesis)]

- **Philosophy, Science & Arts:** Refers to a person who synthesizes—one who brings together disparate ideas, methods, or elements to create a new, cohesive whole.
- **Music:** Refers to a musician who plays, programs, or composes using an electronic synthesizer. [[1](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/synthesist), [2](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/synthesist), [3](https://www.howardgardner.com/synthesizing/syn-connect), [4](https://www.researchprospect.com/how-to-synthesise-sources/), [5](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/synthesist)]

Use frequency data from [Google Books Ngram Viewer](https://books.google.com/ngrams) indicates that "synthesist" is considered a low-frequency word in general English. It experienced a minor surge in the mid-1970s and 1980s, coinciding with the popularization of electronic music synthesizers, but it remains vastly less common than its root words (_synthesis_, _synthesize_, or _synthesizer_). [[1](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/synthesist)]

You said: What did John G. Baker mean when he used the word

When English botanist John G. Baker used the word **synthesist** in 1863, he was using it in a scientific, taxonomical context to describe a specific type of **botanist who classifies plant species by grouping similar variations together** rather than splitting them into endless new species. [[1](https://www.oed.com/dictionary/synthesist_n), [2](https://www.oed.com/dictionary/synthesist_n), [3](https://thedailygardener.org/ota20210113/)]

In 19th-century natural history, Baker meant that a synthesist acts as a "lumper" rather than a "splitter":

The 19th-Century Botanical Debate

During the 1800s, botanists were deeply divided over how to categorize the vast number of plant specimens being collected globally. This created two opposing philosophies:

- **The Splitters (Analysts):** These botanists focused on minor differences between plants. If they found a slight variation in leaf shape or petal color, they would analyze it, declare it a brand-new species, and give it a unique name.
- **The Lumpers (Synthesists):** These botanists—including Baker—focused on broad similarities. They looked at a wide range of variations and gathered ("synthesized") them under a single, overarching species name, treating minor differences as mere local adaptations.

Baker's Definition in Practice

When Baker coined or popularized the term, he meant a **scientific unifier**. To him, a synthesist was a researcher possessing the rare ability to:

- Look past minor, distracting physical variations in specimens.
- Recognize the shared genetic or morphological core of a plant group.
- Bring harmony to messy botanical records by condensing chaotic lists of names into cohesive, well-defined species.

If you want, we can explore **how Baker applied this "lumping" philosophy** to his famous studies of ferns and lilies, or look into how this historical "lumper vs. splitter" debate still **impacts modern DNA-based plant classification** today.
